content: 1. Schünemann HJ, Mustafa R, Brozek J, Santesso N, Alonso-Coello P, Guyatt G, et al. published the GRADE Guidelines: 16, which focus on the GRADE evidence-to-decision frameworks for tests in clinical practice and public health. This was published in the Journal of Clinical Epidemiology in 2016 (Volume 76, Pages 89–98). 2. The World Health Organization (WHO) released a document in 2010 titled Declaration of Interests for WHO Experts, which outlines the ethical and procedural considerations for expert involvement in WHO activities. 3. Dickson R, Awasthi S, Demellweek C, and Williamson P conducted a Cochrane systematic review in 2000 (Issue 2, CD000371) on the effects of anthelmintic drugs for treating worms in children, specifically examining their impact on growth and cognitive performance. 4. Taylor-Robinson DC, Jones AP, and Garner P reviewed the effects of deworming drugs for soil-transmitted intestinal worms in children, focusing on growth and school performance. This Cochrane review was published in 2007 (Issue 4, CD000371). 5. Taylor-Robinson DC, Maayan N, Soares-Weiser K, Donegan S, and Garner P conducted a Cochrane review in 2012 (Issue 11, CD000371) on the effects of deworming drugs for soil-transmitted intestinal worms in children, with a focus on nutritional indicators, hemoglobin levels, and school performance. 6. Awasthi S, Peto R, Read S, Richards SM, Pande V, Bundy D, et al. conducted the DEVTA trial, a cluster-randomized study involving 1 million preschool children in North India. The trial assessed the effects of population deworming every six months with albendazole. The findings were published in The Lancet in 2013 (Volume 381, Pages 1478–1486). 7. Aiken AM, Davey C, Hargreaves JR, and Hayes RJ re-analyzed the health and educational impacts of a school-based deworming program in western Kenya. This pure replication study was published in the International Journal of Epidemiology in 2015 (Volume 44, Pages 1572–1580). 8. Gulani A, Nagpal J, Osmond C, and Sachdev HPS conducted a systematic review of randomized controlled trials to evaluate the effect of intestinal anthelmintic drugs on hemoglobin levels. This review was published in the BMJ in 2007 (Volume 334, Page 1095). 9. Walson JL, Herrin BR, and John-Stewart G reviewed the effects of deworming helminth co-infected individuals on delaying HIV disease progression. This Cochrane review was published in 2009 (Issue 3, CD006419). 10. The Cochrane Collaboration, edited by J. Higgins and S. Green, published an online resource in 2011 detailing systematic review methodologies. 11. WHO guidelines on preventive chemotherapy for controlling soil-transmitted helminth infections in at-risk population groups include recommendations for young children (12–23 months), preschool children (24–59 months), and school-age children (5–12 years). The guidelines emphasize the importance of improving nutrition and health outcomes through deworming interventions, with specific considerations for dose and frequency. 12. Preventive chemotherapy for non-pregnant adolescent girls and women of reproductive age (15–49 years) is recommended in endemic areas to improve nutrition and health outcomes. Subgroup analyses include baseline prevalence of helminth infections, anemia prevalence, and concomitant HIV infection. 13. Preventive chemotherapy for pregnant women in endemic areas is recommended to improve maternal and neonatal health outcomes. Outcomes include maternal anemia, iron deficiency, reinfection rates, maternal mortality, birth weight, and perinatal mortality. 14. The GRADE Working Group provides a framework for assessing the quality of evidence. High-quality evidence indicates strong confidence in the estimated effect, while moderate, low, and very low-quality evidence reflect increasing levels of uncertainty due to factors such as bias, inconsistency, and imprecision. 15. Studies included in the reviews were often downgraded for risks of bias, inconsistency, and indirectness. Common issues included inadequate reporting of allocation concealment, blinding, and baseline imbalances, as well as high heterogeneity in results. 16. The WHO guidelines emphasize the importance of addressing soil-transmitted helminth infections in at-risk populations through evidence-based preventive chemotherapy, with careful consideration of the quality of evidence and contextual factors.
